General Strike Paralyzes Key Sectors Across Ecuador, Disrupting Daily Life and Economy

QUITO – A nationwide general strike has brought much of Ecuador’s economic activity to a standstill, as workers from transport, education, healthcare, and public administration sectors staged coordinated walkouts and protests in major cities on Tuesday. The action, called by the United Workers’ Federation and supported by multiple trade bodies, is ongoing and has led to widespread disruption from the highland capital to the Pacific coast.

In the capital Quito, public transportation was severely curtailed, leaving commuters stranded at bus terminals and long lines forming at taxi stands. “I’ve been waiting for almost two hours and there are no buses. I can’t get to work,” said Maria Jaramillo, a supermarket employee in the north of the city. Many schools and universities suspended classes for the day, citing safety concerns as demonstrations grew in size through the morning.

The Confederation of Health Workers reported that non-urgent medical appointments were postponed in Quito, Guayaquil, and Cuenca, while emergency rooms remained open. “We are maintaining essential services, but the government must address our demands for improved funding and working conditions,” said Dr. Luis Castro, a spokesperson for the confederation.

The general strike is in response to sweeping economic reforms announced by the government last month, including changes to labor laws and subsidy reductions. Protest leaders argue the measures disproportionately impact working-class families. “We are not against modernization, but these policies threaten our livelihoods,” said Rosa Minda, president of the National Teachers’ Union, during a rally outside the Ministry of Labor.

Export activity through the Port of Guayaquil, critical for Ecuador’s banana and shrimp industries, slowed sharply as dockworkers joined the strike. The Ecuadorian Chamber of Commerce estimated that daily losses could exceed $45 million if disruptions continue. “Our members are deeply concerned about the halt in logistics and the impact on international contracts,” said Pedro Villacís, the chamber’s executive director.

Government officials urged calm and called for dialogue. Interior Minister Sofía Lema said in a televised statement, “We respect the right to peaceful protest but urge all parties to avoid violence and disruption to essential services.”

As negotiations between union leaders and the government showed little immediate progress, analysts warned that continuing unrest could damage investor confidence and further strain Ecuador’s fragile economy. The strike is set to continue on Wednesday, with union representatives vowing to maintain pressure until their concerns are addressed.
